description: Group of highly motivated STEM individuals
summary: ATLAS finds places on Earth that match the lighting a rover meets at the Moon's south pole, and tells a test team exactly when the match holds. At the lunar south pole the Sun sits about 1.5° above the horizon and shadows run for kilometres. ATLAS measures the pattern of sunlight and shade along a 500 m route there using NASA LOLA elevation and JPL Horizons Sun positions, then searches Earth for routes where a rover would drive through the same pattern. Our shadow engine agrees with NASA Goddard's own lunar illumination map (r = 0.955 at 600 points). A whole-planet screen using NASA MODIS land cover shows that nowhere closer to the equator than 62° holds the match for a full rover drive, which rules out the famous desert analogs for this test. Without being told about analog sites, the screen found Devon Island, home of NASA's Haughton-Mars Project. Because the heavy shadow work is computed once, our calculator lets a mission change its requirements and re-ranks every candidate without re-running it.
details:
What it does

NASA describes the long, fast-moving shadows at the lunar south pole as a new problem for rover cameras and lights. A test site on Earth needs more than terrain that looks lunar. It needs the Sun at the same low height, from the same direction, for as long as a drive lasts. ATLAS finds those places and the exact days and minutes the match holds.

How it works

1. Moon: we cut a 500 m route near the ridge between Shackleton and de Gerlache craters into 12 segments and measure four things: share in shade, longest shaded stretch, entries into shade, and steepness. Shadows come from horizon profiles on NASA LOLA elevation, with the Sun treated as a disc.

2. Validation: we computed how often each point near the pole sees the Sun and compared it with NASA Goddard's published illumination map: r = 0.955 at 600 points, 139 of NASA's 145 permanently shadowed points matched.

3. Planet screen: for every latitude, a full year of Sun positions, combined with NASA MODIS bare-ground land cover. Only about 740,000 km² of bare ground (3.6%) gets at least 50 usable hours a year, and none of it lies closer to the equator than 62°.

4. Regions: in eight regions we tested about 73,000 routes each on 30 m Copernicus elevation, every 3 minutes through 2027. North-central Baffin Island's best route matches for 76.5 hours a year. Haughton crater matches for 72.5. The Atacama and Jebel Hafeet match for at most 12 minutes at a time, too short for one 42-minute drive.

5. Calculator: the shadow results are computed once, so a mission can change its Sun-height tolerance, slope limit, rover speed and scoring weights and see every candidate re-ranked in the browser. Its results matched our full Python engine in 22 of 22 tests.

Benefits and impact

A rover or camera team can plan a field test on the right ground at the right hour, instead of travelling to a site that only looks lunar.

Creativity

Most analog searches compare places. ATLAS treats an analog as a place and a time, and computes when the match exists.

Factors we considered

We mapped 26 site factors a test team cares about. ATLAS covers 3 today (steepness, Sun angle, sunlight and shade), 16 more have open data available, and 7 need a field visit.

Limits

Nothing smaller than the 30 m elevation grid is visible. Snow and how dark a shadow looks are not modelled. The Moon route is a placeholder that a mission route would replace.

Tools

Python (NumPy, SciPy, Matplotlib, Rasterio), HTML, CSS and JavaScript, D3 and TopoJSON for the globes. Claude (Anthropic) was used for coding, research and writing, as stated on the project page.
